documents.abstract: Multi-UAV emergency monitoring can enlarge spatial coverage, but overlapping fields of view create dependent detections that violate the conditional-independence assumption of conventional Bayesian accumulation. This study presents a correlation-aware method that converts georeferenced neural-detector outputs from multiple unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs) into a calibrated probabilistic emergency map. Detector likelihoods are empirically calibrated, projected detections are distributed over a spatial grid, and repeated observations are down-weighted through an effective sample size derived from viewpoint and temporal similarity. The method is evaluated with a geometrically exact camera simulation and a detector emulator calibrated from 10,463 real annotated frames. In a synthetic model with an exactly computable posterior, correlation-aware fusion reduces the median excess Brier score from 23.4% for naive fusion to 3.9%, and the worst case from 91.5% to 8.2%. In the flight simulation, expected calibration error decreases from 0.046 to 0.013 for tightly clustered viewpoints. A weighted Voronoi coordination layer additionally reduces coverage time by a factor of 3.47 and duplicated imaging from 100% to 10.0% over 1 km² with five UAVs. The results show that explicitly accounting for dependence is important for probabilistic multi-UAV situational awareness.

Vibe coding uses repeated natural-language prompts and minimal code review in large language model (LLM)-based development. Development may end before sufficient client–LLM context co-construction occurs. We propose CO-constructed SPECification (COSPEC), combining Joint Application Development facilitation with Specification by Example. Within a four-stage cycle, the LLM presents prototype scenarios for client review and records approved scenarios as Given–When–Then (GWT) specifications. An automated exploratory evaluation used an LLM client given a reference specification and engagement policies. We conducted 150 runs across five conditions involving COSPEC, GitHub Spec Kit-based Spec-Driven Development (SDD), and vibe coding, varying Claude/Codex role assignments and Maker reasoning levels. Dialogues and artifacts showed client-role revision requests and acceptance reflected in scenarios and GWT specifications. Mean requirements coverage through co-construction favored SDD under diligent engagement and COSPEC under satisficing engagement; significant method differences were limited to particular requirement categories and Judges. Both methods covered more requirements through co-construction under diligent engagement. These observations support the feasibility of delegating specification writing to the LLM while involving clients through repeated responses. However, presentation medium and procedure varied together, preventing isolation of their effects. Whether this supports sustained human participation requires human evaluation.

topics: Generative Adversarial Networks and Image Synthesis

documents.abstract: Abstract Artificial Intelligence has fundamentally changed the modern digital operation, whereby creating a constant struggle between what is perceived to be true and the human reality. This study uses a qualitative, exploratory-descriptive study using secondary data from academic journals, policy documents and institutional reports to examine the interaction between crowdsourced Open-Sourced Intelligence (OSINT) and Artificial Intelligence (AI) driven propaganda in modern warfare, alongside the global governance challenges that arise from their interaction. Findings reveal that there is a serious tension within the digital information ecosystem: whilst generative Artificial Intelligence promotes public opinions to spread disinformation and misinformation that is persuasive and may manipulate political processes, crowdsourced intelligence offers real-time verification and transparency. There are Regulatory Frameworks such as the European Union’s AI Act and Digital Services Act that serve as blueprints to counter AI-driven manipulation from technical solutions to the adoption of human-centered governance models. Ultimately, the study demonstrates that it is important to maintain digital information integrity by balancing computational tools with collaborative human verification to foster resilience against any revolving threats in digital security and global governance. Keywords: Artificial Intelligence, Open-Source Intelligence (OSINT), Crowdsourced Verification, AI-Driven Propaganda, Digital Warfare, Global Governance, Disinformation, Epistemic Sovereignty
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: Decision-making is an indispensable component of business life. As a broad and interdisciplinary field, decision theory and decision-making techniques are examined from different perspectives by various disciplines, each offering distinct solution approaches. The decision-making process involves not only behavioral aspects such as the identification of decision makers, motivation theories, and decision philosophy, but also analytical and quantitative tools including matrices, probability calculations, optimization techniques, artificial intelligence, simulation, and machine learning. In short, hundreds of methods, approaches, tools, and disciplines are directly related to decision theory.

Abstract Transcription factor-based biosensors are essential for the scalable bioproduction of plant natural products. However, a major bottleneck in developing high-performance biosensors is the engineering of responsive promoters due to the vast sequence space and poorly understood sequence–function relationships. Here, we extend our previously published DeepSEED framework into an artificial intelligence-driven pipeline for efficient and extensible biosensor-responsive promoter optimization. This strategy integrates deep learning with domain-specific biological expertise. By fixing core promoter elements, varying the number and position of transcription factor binding sites (TFBSs) to define promoter backbones, and subsequently optimizing the flanking sequences, we enable the de novo design of promoters. We systematically apply this strategy to optimize a panel of biosensors across different transcription factors and regulatory modes, including four metabolite-responsive biosensors and a quorum-sensing-based environmental sensor. The resulting biosensors exhibit diverse dynamic behaviors with markedly improved sensitivity, expanded dynamic range, and increased maximum output. For instance, the optimized naringenin biosensor demonstrates a 32-fold broader dynamic range and a 27-fold higher maximum output compared to its parent. To illustrate its utility in metabolic engineering, we employed a DeepSEED-designed promoter to dynamically regulate a p-coumaric acid biosynthesis pathway, boosting production by 117.0%. Our work extends the previously published DeepSEED framework into a powerful pipeline for biosensor optimization and delivers a portfolio of high-performance regulatory elements, addressing a critical need and facilitating the development of more intelligent and productive metabolic engineering systems.

The massive irruption of generative artificial intelligence (GAI) constitutes an ontological event that challenges contemporary education beyond mere technical efficiency or academic integrity. This study justifies the critical urgency of addressing the structural "groundlessness" of the human person in the face of current algorithmic saturation and technological idolatry. The main objective is to analyze, within the theoretical framework of Sensitive Education, the imminent risk of the "synthetic echo" supplanting the student's "original voice," thereby atrophying their discursive agency and capacity for meaning. A hermeneutic and phenomenological methodology is employed, articulating Leonardo Polo's transcendental anthropology, Hartmut Rosa's sociology of resonance, and the cultural criticism of authors such as Byung-Chul Han and Éric Sadin. The results reveal a deep existential fracture: AI imposes a "perfect closure" of data that collides with human "radical openness," generating an alienation where discourse (logos) is traumatically dissociated from vital experience (bios). In conclusion, it is argued that true digital literacy requires a transition from the isolation of the digital "false-we" towards a "mature-we" capable of ethical resistance and real alterity. Educational assessment must abandon the forensic approach to plagiarism to discern, through a "resonant hearing," the vibratory authenticity of learning, thus guaranteeing the primacy of the spirit over automatism and restoring the classroom as an essential sanctuary of presence and listening.

Virtual reality (VR) games are becoming increasingly popular for entertainment. When integrated into speech and language therapy (SLT) practice, VR can be an innovative tool that supports therapeutic interventions by offering new opportunities for immersive interaction and greater motivation for individuals with language disorders to participate in therapy. In this study, we aim to introduce a methodology for designing interactive VR serious-game scenarios for speech and language therapy, together with an integrated multidisciplinary user-feedback assessment framework. The research methodology is based on design research principles and an innovative UX framework to guide the design, evaluation, and improvement process. The feasibility and usability of the methodology and framework are demonstrated through preliminary interactive sessions involving 10 children and adolescents with language disorders (5–13 years) and 10 students undergoing speech and language therapy. Their role was to evaluate the serious VR games developed in accordance with specific speech and language therapy goals. The assessment framework consists of a four-level VR serious game hub statistics module, phonetic and linguistic analysis of children’s and adolescents’ utterances from the serious game sessions, and usability and design questionnaires. As a result, six VR serious games with integrated large language model (LLM)-based conversational AI were designed for speech and language therapy. Based on the outcomes, a safety protocol for conducting VR-based therapeutic activities was proposed. We used descriptive statistics and Friedman and Wilcoxon post hoc tests with Bonferroni-adjusted p -values for pairwise comparisons of questionnaires and speech and language assessment data. While preliminary, the results of the phonetic and linguistic analyses conducted using Praat indicate that the VR serious games effectively capture and maintain children’s attention, elicit a high level of emotional expressiveness, and motivate them to communicate. The feedback collected through the participant questionnaires showed that the VR serious games provided a highly positive user experience. No symptoms of cybersickness or dizziness were observed during the game sessions. Younger children interacted with the VR environment using controllers, while older individuals preferred interaction with hand gestures. The proposed solution can be personalized to individual therapeutic needs, enabling children with language disorders to be engaged in therapy, while the conversational AI integrated into VR stimulates not only expressive development but also receptive language development. To confirm the promising preliminary results, further evaluations with a larger group of children and longitudinal studies are required.

The rapid integration of artificial intelligence (AI) into education is prompting teacher education programs to reconsider their pedagogical foundations. Many current approaches, however, equate technological adoption with meaningful learning, overlooking deeper epistemological and instructional challenges. This chapter presents the Meaningful AI-Integrated Learning Framework (MAILF), a theoretically grounded model designed for teacher education. Drawing on constructivism, Meaningful Learning Theory, and the TPACK model, MAILF defines four interconnected dimensions: conceptual grounding, critical AI literacy, reflective pedagogical design, and ethical agency. It argues that effective AI integration depends less on technical skills and more on developing educators' critical, reflective, and ethical capacities. The framework positions AI as a cognitive partner that enhances learning. Implications for curriculum design, faculty development, and institutional policy are also discussed.
topics: Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education

documents.abstract: Dyslexia and dyscalculia are lifelong learning disabilities that affect how individuals process language and numbers. Children with these disabilities often require specialized support, which can be difficult and expensive to provide. Smartphones and their applications (apps) have created opportunities for accessible digital learning support. However, most existing educational apps do not support Arabic language. Motivated by this, we introduce Hikaya, an interactive Android application designed to assist children with learning difficulties, particularly in Arabic-speaking countries. Hikaya provides bilingual support in Arabic and English covering three core subjects: Arabic, English, and Math. Parents can create accounts, add children, and monitor progress through a dedicated dashboard. Children can engage with one of three learning models, including a unique Reading Karaoke feature that allows them to read scripts aloud while the app evaluates their performance. To assess Hikaya’s perceived utility, user satisfaction, and system usability, a perception survey was completed by 200 participants after a one-month test period. The results displayed highly positive user reception and strong satisfaction. As future work, we aim to expand Hikaya’s language capabilities by supporting various Arabic dialects and widely spoken global languages. We also plan to integrate adaptive learning algorithms using Artificial Intelligence and collaborate with educators and speech therapists to enhance the app’s learning value.
topics: Assistive Technology in Communication and Mobility
Intelligent Tutoring Systems and Adaptive Learning

documents.abstract: The digital transformation of higher education requires the development of assessment systems capable of measuring not only the amount of knowledge acquired by students but also their ability to understand, apply, analyze, evaluate, and create information in technology-mediated contexts. This article examines the theoretical and methodological foundations for developing criteria and indicators for assessing students’ knowledge in a digital educational environment. The study employs systematic analysis, comparison, classification, synthesis, and pedagogical modelling. The proposed framework includes six assessment criteria: conceptual knowledge, comprehension and interpretation, practical application, analytical and problem-solving ability, knowledge integration and creation, and reflective and self-regulated learning. Each criterion is operationalised through measurable qualitative and quantitative indicators. A four-level assessment scale — advanced, proficient, developing, and insufficient — is introduced to improve transparency and consistency. The article also proposes a weighted formula for calculating an integrated student knowledge score. Particular attention is given to validity, reliability, fairness, transparency, accessibility, academic integrity, and the pedagogically responsible use of learning analytics and artificial intelligence. The findings indicate that digital assessment becomes educationally meaningful when assessment tasks are aligned with learning outcomes, indicators are observable and measurable, students receive timely feedback, and automated data are combined with professional teacher judgement. The proposed framework may be adapted to different university disciplines, learning management systems, and blended or fully online educational programmes.

The rapid advancement of digital technologies and the integration of artificial intelligence (AI) in accounting practices have significantly increased the complexity and uncertainty of professional work environments, making Dynamic Risk Management Skills a critical competency for contemporary accounting graduates. This study aims to examine the relationships between AI Competency and Dynamic Risk Management Skills among Generation Z (Gen Z) accounting students, with Systematic Thinking Ability and Design Thinking Ability considered as mediating variables. A quantitative research design was employed, collecting data from 571 fourth-year accounting students across Thailand. The data were analyzed using partial least squares structural equation modeling (PLS-SEM). The results reveal that AI Competency is significantly and positively associated with Systematic Thinking Ability, Design Thinking Ability, and Dynamic Risk Management Skills. Moreover, Systematic Thinking Ability and Design Thinking Ability significantly account for the indirect associations between AI Competency and Dynamic Risk Management Skills. These findings extend theoretical understanding of risk management skill development in accounting education and offer practical implications for curriculum design by emphasizing the integration of AI with higher-order thinking skill development to better prepare graduates for complex and rapidly changing professional environments.

Current study focuses on developing conductive weft-knitted fabrics with electromagnetic shielding properties for potential use in ergonomic maternity clothing. Conductive core-spun yarns were produced by wrapping 40 µm stainless steel wires with cotton fibers via ring spinning and knitted into single jersey, rib (1×1), and interlock structures. The fabrics' electromagnetic shielding effectiveness (EMSE) and surface resistivity were tested across 0.1 to 3 GHz. Fabrics with higher conductive yarn content showed lower surface resistivity (down to 6.54 × 10⁴ Ω) and higher EMSE, with the best-performing sample achieving 10.09 dB. Shielding effectiveness was strongest at lower frequencies, gradually decreasing as frequency increased. Interlock and rib structures outperformed single jersey due to their denser configurations. Building on these results, a conceptual collection of ergonomic maternity dresses was suggested, emphasizing protection, comfort, sustainability, and the needs of pregnant women.

The assessment of vibration signals in automotive generators is crucial for ensuring operational efficiency, reliability and predictive maintenance. Excessive vibrations can lead to mechanical failures, energy losses and reduced generator lifespan. However, traditional vibration monitoring methods often rely on periodic manual inspections, which are time-consuming, expensive and inefficient for real-time diagnostics. To address this issue, this study focuses on the development of an IoT-based system for real-time vibration signal assessment in automotive generators. The methodology involves designing and implementing a wireless sensor network integrated with microcontrollers and accelerometers to capture vibration signals continuously. The collected data is transmitted to a cloud-based platform for real-time processing and analysis using machine learning algorithms. The system employs edge computing techniques to enhance data processing speed and reduce latency. A prototype is tested in a controlled environment to evaluate its performance in detecting abnormal vibration patterns and predicting potential faults. The justification for this study lies in the increasing demand for intelligent and automated monitoring solutions in modern automotive power systems. By leveraging IoT technology, this research provides a cost-effective, scalable, and efficient alternative to conventional vibration monitoring techniques, contributing to improved energy efficiency and reliability of generators. The results demonstrate that the developed IoT system effectively detects and analyzes vibration anomalies in real time, enabling early fault detection and reducing maintenance costs. In conclusion, the proposed system enhances the predictive maintenance capabilities of automotive generators, ensuring longer operational life and reduced downtime. It was recommended that future research explore the integration of advanced artificial intelligence models for more accurate predictive analytics and the implementation of this system in real-world automotive applications to validate its robustness and scalability.

Background: Ductal carcinoma in situ (DCIS) may be upstaged to invasive carcinoma after surgical excision. Predicting upstaging before surgery may help guide treatment planning. Artificial intelligence (AI)-based imaging has been investigated for this purpose, but its overall performance remains unclear. Objective: To evaluate the diagnostic accuracy of AI-based systems for predicting DCIS upstaging to invasive carcinoma. Materials and Methods: A systematic review and meta-analysis was conducted following PRISMA 2020 and registered in PROSPERO (CRD420261516994). PubMed, Scopus, EBSCOhost, ProQuest, and Web of Science were searched from inception to September 2026. Studies evaluating AI-based imaging models for DCIS upstaging were included. Pooled sensitivity and specificity were calculated using a bivariate random-effects model. Risk of bias was assessed using QUADAS-2. Results: Six studies involving 701 participants were included. Pooled sensitivity was 0.77 (95% CI, 0.57–0.89) and specificity was 0.78 (95% CI, 0.64–0.87), with substantial heterogeneity (I² = 84.0% and 90.6%, respectively). The pooled log diagnostic odds ratio (DOR) was 2.15 (95% CI, 1.64–2.65). The SROC analysis showed moderate overall discriminative performance. No significant differences were observed across imaging modalities, while AI model type significantly affected specificity but not sensitivity. Deeks’ funnel plot suggested possible publication bias (p = 0.046). Conclusion: AI-based imaging showed moderate accuracy for predicting DCIS upstaging. However, substantial heterogeneity and methodological limitations limit confidence in these findings. Further prospective studies with external validation are needed.
topics: Radiomics and Machine Learning in Medical Imaging

documents.abstract: This article examines learners’ use of artificial intelligence (AI) with both languagerelated and subject-specific learning processes in the foreign language classroom. The development of critical digital literacy (#CDL), understood as the ability to critically assess and evaluate digital, including AI-generated content, is focused on in the reported research data, a video-taped double lesson of an upper-secondary advanced English course. In the lesson, learners used generative AI ChatGPT and DALL-E 3) to design their own campaigns for the promotion of gender equality, and discussed and reflected the appropriateness of AI-generated visual representations. The data analysis draws on video and screen recordings, group discussions, the plenary presentation and the subsequently initiated reflection. Focusing on a critical incident, the analysis shows how learners negotiate meaning by aligning with or distancing themselves from AI-generated artefacts, concomitantly developing, testing, evaluating and reflecting upon prompting strategies. In particular, the data reveal the learners’ critical engagement with AI-generated representations of gender in relation to diversity, equality, justice and intersectional equity as well as implicit and contested beauty ideals. Processes of interpretation, appropriation, emotional engagement and the act of developing and defending a position become visible as learners distance themselves from DALL-E 3’s stereotypical visual worlds and the underlying algorithmic biases of ChatGPT.

Purpose This study maps knowledge production in digital circular economy research across an eight-year period. It examines which themes achieve prominence, and at what stage of publication that prominence is established. Design/methodology/approach The study analysed 1,803 Scopus-indexed journal articles and reviews published between 2017 and 2024. Descriptive bibliometrics and keyword co-occurrence were produced in bibliometrix via Biblioshiny, and thematic classification in Text Analysis for All. Citation counts were then modelled in R by negative binomial regression, controlling for year, document type, team size and journal. Findings Technical and optimisation vocabulary appears in 67.6% of documents once terms shared with the search query are excluded. The share is 79.9% when those overlapping terms are retained in the lexicon. Social and governance vocabulary appears in 21.5% of documents, and distributive vocabulary in 3.5%. Thematic classification produces six clusters of moderate stability, none of which is organised around distributive vocabulary. Socially oriented documents receive 58% fewer citations than technically oriented documents after controls for year, type and team size. This difference attenuates to 50% once the citation level of the publishing journal is taken into account. Holding journal identity constant reduces the difference further, to a level not distinguishable from zero. Journal placement therefore accounts for between a fifth and three-fifths of the difference, depending on how venue is measured. The analysis reported throughout identifies a statistical association rather than a demonstrated causal mechanism. Originality/value The study applies work on sociotechnical imaginaries to a stage that earlier accounts have not examined. Academic publishing narrows the range of available framings before policy or infrastructure takes shape. It also separates geographic representation from thematic diversity, two properties that authorship counts alone conflate.

Introduction The Digital Health Africa 2025 Conference (DHA-2025, https://digitalhealthafrica.org/ ) addressed the integration of digital tools within critical global health priorities, including maternal and child health (MCH), antimicrobial resistance artificial intelligence (AI), and pharmacometrics. While the adoption of digital health shows immense potential for improving healthcare access in Africa’s resource-limited environments, its practical application in the public sector remains sub-optimal due to policy misalignment and inadequate systemic investments. Digital health interventions can achieve sustained, large-scale impact when properly supported, as demonstrated by successful platforms like MomConnect in South Africa and MomCare in Kenya. However, successfully scaling these systems beyond initial pilots requires a robust foundation built on three pillars: technical capacity (infrastructure), legal legitimacy (regulation), and effective management (governance). Furthermore, while advanced tools like AI and pharmacometric modeling are now practical realities in healthcare in developed countries, the most significant challenge remains operationalizing and transitioning these sophisticated tools safely from the laboratory to the clinical bedside in Africa. Conclusion Scientific advancement in digital health is insufficient on its own; the true test of innovation lies in its safe and practical integration into end-user healthcare delivery. To successfully scale digital health solutions in resource-constrained settings, stakeholders must prioritize cross-continental collaborations, invest heavily in capacity building, and secure long-term commitments to infrastructure and policy development.
topics: Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education

documents.abstract: This research paper explains the transformation of traditional libraries into digital libraries due to the rapid development of Information and Communication Technology (ICT). The paper discusses the concept, need, major features, benefits, and limitations of digital libraries. It also describes modern services provided through digital libraries, including online reference services, e-reference services, Selective Dissemination of Information (SDI), Current Awareness Services (CAS), e-book and e-journal services, digital repositories, OPAC/Web OPAC, document delivery services, inter-library loan and resource sharing, mobile library services, QR code-based services, plagiarism detection, reference management, AI-based information services, and digital literacy services. In addition, the application of modern technologies such as cloud computing, Artificial Intelligence, Machine Learning, Generative AI, Optical Character Recognition (OCR), Natural Language Processing (NLP), Big Data Analytics, Internet of Things (IoT), RFID, Blockchain, Knowledge Graphs, Linked Data, Semantic Web, Open Access Repositories, mobile technologies, and chatbots in digital libraries is discussed. Finally, the paper highlights the future directions of digital libraries, the concept of smart knowledge centres, and the changing role of librarians.
topics: Library Collection Development and Digital Resources

documents.abstract: The article examines digital diaspora lobbying as an organizational and communicative process linking collective interests with their presentation to decision-making institutions. It aims to clarify the functional relationship between representation, social media, narrative diplomacy and artificial intelligence, and to propose a conceptual model of the main stages of this process. The study is based on an analytical review of selected scientific literature, conceptual comparison and functional modeling. Five foundations of diaspora representation are identified: defining the represented community, agreeing on common interests, granting representative authority, ensuring internal participation and maintaining accountability. The model includes six stages: defining the mandate, specifying the problem and evidence base, preparing the narrative and institutional proposal, public communication, engagement with decision-making institutions, and evaluation of results. Artificial intelligence supports data classification, source search, multilingual drafting and document comparison, while collective decision-making and public responsibility remain with the organization. Results are assessed through communicative visibility, trust and institutional response. The proposed framework links these levels to specific stages and traceable outputs and requires further empirical verification.

The rapid development of Artificial Intelligence (AI) is transforming Translation Studies (TS). This article adopts a historical and critical approach, based on a literature review from 1954 to 2024, from Statistical Machine Translation to Generative AI. While Generative Translation (GT) achieves unprecedented fluency and terminological consistency, it still fails to render cultural depth, ethical nuance and spiritual meaning. Through examples such as the translation of 仁 (Ren) and رحمة (Rahma), the study argues that the translator's role is evolving from a linguistic transferer to a cultural guarantor and strategic curator of meaning. The paper concludes that Human Translation is not doomed, but its survival depends on integrating AI mastery with intercultural mediation, in line with the Global Civilization Initiative. Article submitted to Frontiers (ID 2030041) on 15-10-2026. Deposited on Zenodo in Restricted Access for author copyright protection.

Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly embedded in enterprise platforms, yet the ability to access an AI-enabled technology does not necessarily imply readiness to adopt it. This study examines whether digital skills readiness operates as a human-capital antecedent of AI-enabled enterprise technology adoption intention and whether technology readiness and performance expectancy transmit that relationship. The study follows the supplied IBM-group research plan and analyses the 385 populated cases in the accompanying master database. The questionnaire contains three-item measures for Digital Skills Readiness, Technology Readiness, Performance Expectancy and Adoption Intention, alongside additional adoption constructs. Because the supplied database contains 385 complete populated cases and 15 unused template rows, the analysis retains the 385 populated observations and applies an attention-check screen. The empirical strategy combines measurement diagnostics, descriptive analysis, correlation analysis, standardized composite path modeling and 5,000-resample bootstrap mediation analysis. The results show a positive association between Digital Skills Readiness and Technology Readiness (β = .392, p < .001), a positive association between Technology Readiness and Performance Expectancy (β = .195, p < .001), and positive effects of Digital Skills Readiness, Technology Readiness and Performance Expectancy on Adoption Intention (β = .174, .248 and .268, respectively; all p ≤ .001). The serial indirect effect from Digital Skills Readiness through Technology Readiness and Performance Expectancy to Adoption Intention is positive (indirect effect ≈ .020, 95% bootstrap CI [.008, .035]). The model explains 15.4% of variance in Technology Readiness, 4.6% in Performance Expectancy and 23.7% in Adoption Intention. However, the measurement diagnostics reveal weak internal consistency and convergent validity for several supplied three-item scales, including Digital Skills Readiness and Technology Readiness. Accordingly, the structural results should be interpreted as evidence from composite-score diagnostics rather than as a final confirmatory latent-variable model. The study contributes a capability-to-readiness-to-appraisal mechanism for understanding AI-enabled enterprise adoption in an emerging-market setting and identifies measurement refinement as a necessary next step before Q1 journal submission.

This article theorizes phatic imbalances as emergent effects of how participation and presence are reorganized in contemporary digital sociality. It argues that participation in digital networks has become increasingly transactional and positional, oriented toward sustaining visibility and availability rather than exchanging meaning. Drawing on work on networked sociality, weak ties and deep mediatization, the article conceptualizes phaticity and phatic work as priori conditions of digital participation. It introduces digital proxemics as the sociotechnical production of presence, distance and relational positioning in environments structured by telepresence, virtuality and AI-infused affordances. Phatic imbalances arise when infrastructural demands for continuous phatic presence exceed the cognitive and temporal capacities of subjects, producing overload, hollowed presence and machine-modulated rhythms of interaction. By linking participation, phaticity and digital proxemics, the article offers a diagnostic lens for understanding how digital infrastructures reshape attention, presence and communicative agency in AI-saturated environments.

This chapter examines digital storytelling as a powerful tool for advancing inclusive pedagogy in higher education. Drawing on frameworks including critical pedagogy, universal design for learning (UDL), culturally relevant pedagogy, and participatory culture theory, it argues that social media platforms can function as sites of equity-oriented learning when intentionally designed. Digital storytelling, defined as the integration of narrative with multimedia elements such as video, audio, and images, enables students to connect course concepts to lived experience, thereby deepening comprehension, fostering agency, and amplifying marginalized voices. Synthesizing existing literature and classroom-based practices, the chapter highlights how social media environments can support participatory learning, identity expression, and community formation, particularly for students who may feel excluded in traditional academic spaces. Empirical examples demonstrate how multimodal storytelling assignments, such as short-form social media videos, enhance engagement, motivation, and sociological imagination while offering flexible modes of expression aligned with UDL principles. The chapter also explores the emerging role of generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) in digital storytelling, emphasizing its potential to lower technical and creative barriers, support multilingual learners, and expand access to multimedia production. At the same time, it critically addresses limitations related to narrative depth, bias, and ethical concerns in human–artificial intelligence (AI) collaboration. Finally, the chapter identifies key risks, including digital inequality, platform surveillance, and emotional vulnerability, and offers practical strategies for ethical and inclusive implementation. Overall, it positions digital storytelling as a transformative pedagogical approach that bridges creativity, accessibility, and social justice in contemporary education.

The rapid advancement of smart technologies is reshaping higher education institutions and creating new pathways for participation in the digital economy. At the same time, ensuring gender inclusion within digitally transforming education systems has become essential for achieving equitable and sustainable development. This chapter examines the role of smart technologies such as artificial intelligence, digital learning platforms, cloud computing, and data-driven education systems in promoting gender-inclusive digital economies within higher education institutions in Brazil. The chapter discusses how technology-enabled education can improve access to learning, strengthen digital skills, and enhance women’s participation in technology-driven sectors. It further explores the opportunities created by digital transformation for inclusive education, as well as the technological, social, institutional, and skills-related barriers that may limit gender-equitable participation. Placing the discussion in the framework of the digital transformation efforts in Brazil, the chapter delineates the increased significance of universities as the source of digital inclusion and the ability to innovate. Future directions associated with digital education ecosystems, women digital empowerment, and inclusive innovation are also described. On the whole, the chapter highlights the idea that, although smart technologies have a great potential in enhancing gender inclusion, maintenance of inclusive digital economies means that attention to access, skill building, and equal participation in the systems of higher education should be consistent.

Digital transformation is reshaping academic libraries through technologies such as ICT, cloud computing, artificial intelligence, mobile applications, digital repositories, and automated systems. These tools improve resource access, routine operations, information discovery, research support, and user services. This review examines current digital transformation trends, their effects on library services, major benefits, implementation challenges, and strategies for sustainable development. Key challenges include limited infrastructure and funding, inadequate staff skills, cybersecurity risks, privacy concerns, copyright issues, the digital divide, and resistance to change. The review concludes that successful transformation requires suitable technology, skilled professionals, supportive policies, adequate infrastructure, and attention to the changing needs of students, teachers, and researchers.
topics: Library Collection Development and Digital Resources

documents.abstract: Digital transformation has become a fundamental driver of healthcare innovation, particularly within hospital pharmacy services. Technologies such as electronic prescribing, barcode medication administration (BCMA), automated dispensing cabinets (ADCs), robotic dispensing systems, artificial intelligence (AI), clinical decision support systems (CDSS), and integrated pharmacy information systems have significantly reshaped pharmacy workflows. These innovations enhance medication safety, improve operational efficiency, and foster interdisciplinary collaboration. This review examines the influence of digital transformation on hospital pharmacy team performance, emphasizing productivity, communication, medication safety, workload distribution, and patient outcomes. Current evidence indicates that digital technologies reduce medication errors, increase dispensing accuracy, optimize inventory management, and improve staff satisfaction. Nevertheless, implementation challenges— including high costs, cybersecurity risks, resistance to organizational change, and training requirements—remain barriers to widespread adoption. Successful digital transformation requires strategic planning, continuous workforce education, leadership commitment, and robust evaluation metrics.

This study examines the professional standing of tourist guides, key actors in the tourism sector, in the context of automation, robotics, and generative artificial intelligence (AI). The empirical framework draws on semi-structured interviews conducted in 2018 with 16 professional tourist guides actively working in Istanbul, alongside responses generated by the ChatGPT-4.1 large language model in 2026 to parallel qualitative research questions. A comparative descriptive analysis reveals both significant convergences and divergences between the two data sources. The findings indicate that 56.25% of human guides and AI agree that automation will quantitatively reduce the need for human guides in routine and information-oriented tours. However, while AI anticipates market segmentation across economic categories, 62.50% of human guides emphasize the human dimension of cultural transmission and do not perceive technology as a direct professional threat. Both sources converge on the view that empathy, emotional connection, humor, flexibility, and storytelling remain difficult to replace through robotic systems. The most notable divergence concerns outdoor guiding: human guides considered it impossible, whereas AI predicted that 5G, GPS, and smart city infrastructures could enable AI-guided outdoor services within 2–5 years. Overall, the study proposes a complementary hybrid service model in which AI assumes operational tasks while human guides focus on cultural interpretation and professional job crafting. It also offers implications for tourism education and digital transformation strategies.

In recent times, the medical world has been dealing with a very serious challenge detecting diseases early enough before they become life-threatening. Many patients, especially in developing countries like Nigeria, only come to know they have a chronic disease when it has already progressed to an advanced and harder-to-treat stage. This is mostly because traditional methods of diagnosis rely heavily on doctors and laboratory technicians manually reviewing test results, a process that can be slow, expensive, and sometimes prone to human error, especially in environments with limited medical personnel or equipment. This work investigates how Artificial Neural Networks (ANN), which is a core technique in the field of machine learning and artificial intelligence, can be trained to automatically predict whether a patient has diabetes based on certain routine medical examination inputs. The work makes use of the widely accepted Pima Indians Diabetes Dataset, which contains the medical records of female patients of Pima Indian heritage, including features such as glucose concentration, blood pressure, body mass index (BMI), age, insulin level, skin thickness, number of pregnancies, and a diabetes pedigree function score. The ANN model was designed with three hidden layers, batch normalization, and dropout regularization to ensure it generalized well on unseen data. After complete training and evaluation on the test portion of the dataset, the model achieved a Test Accuracy of 73.38%, Precision of 59.70%, Recall (Sensitivity) of 74.07%, an F1-Score of 66.12%, and an AUC-ROC score of 0.798. The relatively high Recall score is especially important in a medical context because it means the model successfully identified the majority of actual diabetic patients. These results confirm that Artificial Neural Networks are a highly promising tool for disease prediction and early diagnosis in clinical settings. The simulation was implemented entirely in Python using TensorFlow and Keras, and all results are verifiable from the charts included in this report.

documents.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly promoted as a transformative force in journalism, yet most research on newsroom AI adoption remains concentrated in Western and other well-resourced media settings. This study examines how AI is interpreted, organized, and used in Malaysian newsrooms, offering insight from an emerging Southeast Asian media context. Drawing on semi-structured interviews with 20 journalists across six Malaysian news organizations, the article investigates how national AI governance signals are translated into newsroom norms, how organizational resources and managerial priorities shape uptake, and how AI is incorporated into everyday reporting, editing, and verification. The analysis shows that AI adoption in Malaysian newsrooms is uneven and selective rather than uniform. First, national AI momentum has not yet produced strong newsroom-level governance; instead, the practice remains shaped by limited written rules, selective disclosure, and strong human accountability. Second, organizational capacity is patchy, with uneven access to tools, training, and infrastructural support across organizations and roles. Third, AI is used mainly in bounded, assistive tasks such as transcription, translation, summarization, and headline generation, while verification labor is redistributed rather than reduced. The findings identify a typology of newsroom responses—cautious minimalists, experimental pragmatists, and human-gated adopters—showing that Malaysian newsrooms are not simply “jumping on the AI bandwagon,” but engaging AI pragmatically under uneven governance and resource conditions.

The article analyses five doctrinal problems in applying copyright to literary works created by artificial intelligence (AI). First, it shows that the classical theories (Locke’s labour theory, Hegel’s personality theory, the utilitarian theory and the fair remuneration theory) come into conflict when applied to AI activity. Second, it examines the concept of “author” under the legislation of Uzbekistan, Russia and the United States and under the Berne Convention, together with the question of AI subjecthood. Third, it addresses the originality requirement, fourth, moral rights, and fifth, the idea–expression dichotomy. The author concludes that all these problems share a single cause: classical doctrines rest on human consciousness, will and personality. Accordingly, AI should be treated as a tool rather than a subject. The article also proposes the “objective control criterion doctrine”, which ties the emergence of copyright to objective, verifiable criteria: purposeful direction of AI activity, creative selection among outputs, and determination of the work’s final content and form.

Abstract Knowledge graph question answering (KGQA) aims to answer natural language questions by grounding them in structured knowledge graphs (KGs). Current KGQA systems still face three linked challenges: representing complex and compositional questions, providing transparent multi-hop reasoning traces, and using complete path-level evidence rather than only local triples. We propose SK-DRP ( S yntax- K nowledge enhanced D ynamic R easoning with P rompt learning), a modular KGQA framework that combines syntax-aware representation, state-adaptive path reasoning, and LLM-assisted answer selection. The syntax- and knowledge-enhanced encoder is an auxiliary representation enhancement that uses dependency information and knowledge-augmented pre-training to align questions with KG entities and relations. Here, dynamic denotes hop-wise recomputation of the question-focus indicator, score-qualified frontier expansion, and hop-weighted answer aggregation within a fixed dataset-level maximum hop budget; it does not denote automatic per-question depth selection. Candidate global paths are then compressed and transformed into natural-language auxiliary evidence for candidate-set-guided LLM answer selection. Experiments on MetaQA, WebQSP, and CWQ show that SK-DRP improves over several path-based and retrieval-based baselines on WebQSP and CWQ, while remaining competitive on MetaQA. Ablation, error, and interpretability analyses clarify how the syntax encoder, dynamic reasoning module, and LLM-assisted answer selection contribute to the final results, as well as the scope and limitations of the approach.

Introduction An evidence-guided explainable framework, E-MDD, is developed to integrate high-dimensional EEG representations, neurophysiological biomarkers, and large language models for the recognition of EEG-based depression with concise and evidence-based textual explanations. Methods The proposed E-MDD framework consists of three stages: classification, evidence construction, and evidence-guided inference. In the classification stage, two parallel feature extraction branches are employed to extract Electroencephalography latent features and neurophysiological biomarkers, which are subsequently fused and fed into a lightweight multilayer perceptron for the recognition of depression. In the evidence construction stage, the latent feature dimensions of the EEG are aligned with neurophysiological biomarkers, and the model's decision basis is identified to construct structured evidence supporting the classification results. In the evidence-guided inference stage, structured evidence and the proposed evidence-guided prompt are used to guide the large language model in generating concise textual explanations. Results The experimental results on the Mumtaz dataset show that E-MDD achieves an AUC of 0.8472 and an F1-score of 0.8421. Meanwhile, the generated short-text explanations can effectively describe the basis of the model's decision-making for its predictions, demonstrating a high degree of faithfulness. The proposed framework also demonstrates consistent evidence-guided explanation performance across EEGNet and EEGConformer. Discussion Overall, this study proposes a neurophysiologically interpretable framework for EEG-based deep learning models, which effectively enhances the interpretability of deep learning models for depression detection and provides a new perspective for understanding their decision-making mechanisms.

Electroencephalography (EEG) provides a promising physiological modality for biometric authentication due to its inherent neural uniqueness and resistance to spoofing attacks. However, reliable EEG-based authentication remains challenging because brain signals are highly non-stationary and vary across cognitive states. To address this limitation, this study proposes a multi-paradigm neurophysiological measurement protocol designed to capture stable subject-specific EEG signatures across diverse brain conditions. EEG signals were recorded from participants during six complementary paradigms, including eyes-open and eyes-closed resting states, left and right-hand motor tasks, working-memory encoding, steady-state visual evoked potentials (SSVEP), and steady-state auditory evoked potentials (SSAEP). The recorded signals were preprocessed and segmented into 2-s epochs with 50% overlap. We extracted 28 quantitative descriptors per channel from time, frequency, time-frequency, and nonlinear domains. These descriptors were used to evaluate several decision models, including Mahalanobis distance-based template matching, logistic regression (LR), support vector machine, random forest, and a one-dimensional convolutional neural network. The performance of the proposed measurement system was analyzed under both single-paradigm and multi-paradigm configurations using cross-session validation. Experimental results show that the multi-paradigm measurement protocol reduces the equal error rate (EER) by 2% compared with single-paradigm systems. The LR decision model achieved the best performance with an EER of 1.6% (95% confidence interval: 1.48−1.73), with false rejection rates of 2.06% and 9.01% at false acceptance rates of 1% and 0.1%, respectively. Feature analysis indicated that Hjorth mobility and Mel-frequency cepstral coefficients derived from fronto-central cortical channels provide the most reliable neural identity descriptors. These results demonstrate that multi-paradigm EEG acquisition improves the stability of neural measurements across cognitive states and enables reliable biometric authentication in dynamic conditions.

Background Hospital financial management is facing ongoing challenges. Although artificial intelligence (AI) and robotic process automation (RPA) have shown their potential, there is still a lack of empirical evidence of the effectiveness of the integration of the two in the financial operations of hospitals. This study aims to evaluate the application effect of a set of an AI-RPA integrated intelligent financial system in a large hospital in China. Methods This single-center, non-randomized, uncontrolled before-and-after study was carried out in a large tertiary A general hospital in China from January to December 2025. As an intervention, the intelligent AI-RPA financial system launched in June 2025 consists of four levels: data governance, business processing, technology application and risk control. The study compared the 6 months before the system was launched and the 6 months after the system was launched, in terms of operational efficiency (daily data collection time, report generation time, and automated processing time per transaction), data quality and risk control (data docking success rate, data entry error rate, logical conflict correction rate, and risk prediction accuracy for medical insurance violations) and health-care staff satisfaction. Results After the system went online, the daily data collection time was shortened from 132.5 to 18.6 min ( P < 0.001); the report generation time was shortened from 58.4 to 5.8 min ( P < 0.001); the automated processing time of each transaction was reduced from 3.5 to 1.9 s ( P < 0.001). Data interfacing success rate increased from 94.2 to 99.7%, data entry error rate dropped from 3.5 to 0.6%, logic conflict correction rate rose from 78.1 to 98.5%, and risk prediction accuracy for insurance violations improved from 72.1 to 89.3%. Total staff satisfaction score improved from 30.1 to 43.1 ( P < 0.001). Conclusion This study provides preliminary empirical evidence that the AI-RPA integrated intelligent financial system was associated with improvements in operational efficiency, data quality, risk control, and user satisfaction in a large Chinese hospital.

documents.abstract: This mixed-methods study investigated Omani EFL university students' engagement, motivation, and perceptions of the Spark digital platform in a blended learning context. Using Self-Determination Theory (SDT), the Technology Acceptance Model (TAM), and the Motivated Strategies for Learning Questionnaire (MSLQ) frameworks, the study analyzed survey data, platform analytics, and focus group discussions from 100 students. The results showed that extrinsic, grade-oriented motivation mainly led to moderate engagement. Although analytics suggested high activity, qualitative findings revealed frustration, redundancy, and time pressure. Students reported moderate levels of satisfaction. The study identifies an engagement-compliance paradox, where observable use masks low intrinsic motivation, and recommends a shift to structured in-class use, targeted curriculum alignment, and AI-powered feedback to achieve meaningful and sustained learner engagement.

This essay comparatively analyzes the implementation of transformational leadership in two distinct educational contexts: the Adolfo Jurado Gonz?lez Basic Education School in Ecuador and private K12 schools in China. Through the analysis of Tomal?'s (2025) thesis and Hou, Ahmad, and Zhao's (2024) systematic review, the similarities and differences in applied theoretical models, leadership dimensions, challenges faced, and results obtained in both countries are examined. Both contexts share the adoption of Bass's (1985) model as the fundamental theoretical basis, confirming the positive impact of transformational leadership on teaching practice, intrinsic motivation, and pedagogical innovation. However, while Ecuador focuses on Bass's four classic dimensions (idealized influence, inspirational motivation, intellectual stimulation, and individualized consideration) within a public system focused on educational equity, China diversifies its theoretical approach by incorporating the models of Kouzes and Posner (2006), Bennis and Nanus (1985), and Leithwood and Sun (2012), adapting to a massive and highly competitive private education market. The identified challenges reveal convergences in communication problems, training, and resistance to change, but also significant differences: Ecuador faces technological gaps and economic resource limitations, while China struggles with the cultural adaptation of Western theories, clarification of roles between management and leadership, and demographic pressures. Methodologically, Ecuador uses a quantitative empirical approach with primary data from a specific school, while China employs a systematic literature review with national scope. Results in Ecuador show high levels of teacher satisfaction (91% trust and respect, 100% commitment), while China emphasizes the need to develop culturally adapted theoretical frameworks of its own. Recommendations from both studies converge on the importance of continuous training and feedback, but diverge in that Ecuador prioritizes practical mechanisms coordinated with existing institutions, while China seeks to build specific theories and strategies for its context. The essay concludes that transformational leadership, although universal in its fundamental principles, requires significant contextual adaptations to be effective in educational realities as diverse as those of Ecuador and China.

AI agents can change information when they exchange messages or complete long tasks. A value can be rounded. A location can change. An agent can use an observation from the wrong date. These errors can change decisions about the physical world. emem is an external memory protocol for AI agents. It uses content-addressed evidence records instead of paraphrases. An encoder creates a record from source information. An emem token identifies that record. A compatible receiving agent can resolve the token, decode the record, and check its contents. These operations do not depend on the AI model that sent the reference. Method This poster extends our earlier research on the emem protocol. We use a Sentinel-2A Level-2A observation from Keylong, India, dated 25 September 2026. The selected pixel has a normalized difference vegetation index (NDVI) of 0.4709. We compare four handoff methods: prose, JSON, an opaque identifier, and a checked emem reference. We introduce controlled errors in values, spatial identity, time, source information, derivation, and record integrity. A deterministic receiver checks the record through these steps: Resolve the reference. Recompute the content hash. Check the observation identity. Verify the signature and log. Recompute the measurement when possible. Read the original source data independently when required. Results The deterministic receiver acted on corrupted evidence in 15 of 15 prose handoffs. With the complete emem verification sequence, it acted on none of 16 tested corruptions. We also found an error in emem's earlier satellite pixel reader. In 162 of 200 sampled records, the old reader selected a neighbouring pixel. We corrected the reader on 28 September 2026. None of 54 sampled records after the correction showed this error. The affected records had valid signatures. Thus, a valid signature established record integrity but did not establish measurement correctness. We also checked 780 records. All 780 passed the record-integrity and identity checks. Of these, 266 were recomputed bit for bit. Additional tests examine historical evidence, forest-screening inputs, foundation-model embeddings, and client interoperability. Verification limits A content address identifies exact record bytes. It does not establish physical truth. The records name their source files but do not include cryptographic hashes of those files. The current implementation also depends on keys managed by one operator. The protocol cannot independently establish the sensor's accuracy, the entity intended by the user, or the correctness of a final decision. An AI model can also fail if it removes a reference or ignores a verification refusal. These limits are part of the reported results. Contribution This work separates evidence integrity from measurement accuracy and decision correctness. It shows how AI agents can exchange exact evidence references across different systems. Each receiver can apply checks appropriate to its task. The protocol can also identify foundation-model embeddings as records. emem does not require a specific foundation model or encoder to remain in service. The demonstrated observations in this study come from existing Earth observation archives. Encoding directly at a capture device is a future application, not a result claimed in this poster. Research context Prepared for Agentic AI for Earth Observation, ESA Φ-lab and BIFOLD, Berlin, 19 October 2026. This poster is a companion to the original emem research paper. Original research: Kumari, J., and Singh, A. S. (2026). emem: A research on Content-Addressed, Verifiable Earth-Memory Protocol for AI Agents over Foundation-Model Embeddings. Zenodo, version 0.1.0. DOI: https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.20706893 Poster, methods, and reproducibility materials: https://github.com/Vortx-AI/esa_poster Protocol implementation: https://github.com/Vortx-AI/emem Project: https://emem.dev

Observation is a fundamental scientific practice in science learning, particularly for understanding gradual biological phenomena such as plant adaptation. Despite the increasing integration of artificial intelligence (AI) in education, limited research has examined how AI-supported tools influence students' observation practices during authentic scientific inquiry. This study investigates the emergence and development of students' observation practices during plant adaptation learning supported by an AI-based identifier. A six-week mixed-methods exploratory study was conducted with 84 middle school students. Learning activities were organised into four phases: orientation, initial observation, AI-assisted identification, and re-observation and validation. Data were collected through observation sheets, students' observation notes, reflective journals, group discussions, and records of AI use. Quantitative analysis revealed significant differences in observation orientations across learning phases (Friedman test, p < .001), indicating changes in observation practices over time. Qualitative findings showed that students initially relied on AI-generated cues to guide their observations. Over time, however, observation practices shifted toward direct empirical observation and peer-supported validation through repeated comparisons of plant characteristics across environmental conditions. The findings reveal a developmental trajectory from AI-reliant observation to direct observation and collaborative validation, accompanied by a gradual reduction in dependence on AI-generated outputs. These findings suggest that AI may function as an initial observational scaffold, while more sophisticated observation practices emerge through repeated engagement with phenomena and collaborative reasoning.

Purpose This systematic review analyzed 46 peer-reviewed studies published between 2020 and 2025, revealing eight digital technology types, including Information and Communication Technology, Big Data, Artificial Intelligence, ChatGPT, Open Educational Resources, Massive Open Online Courses, Learning Management System, and Augmented Reality/Virtual Reality. Design/Approach/Method Technologies are organized across three conceptual layers: Infrastructure, Algorithm, and Application Layer. This study aims to investigate: (a) the key functions and implementation barriers of eight emerging technology types; (b) their impacts on teachers’ autonomy, competence, and relatedness; and (c) their impacts on the equity, quality, and efficiency of scalable teacher professional development. Findings Findings reveal that all technologies demonstrate dual impacts on the three psychological needs, both enabling and constraining, with competence most consistently supported across layers. Equity outcomes prove most challenging. Originality/Value This review concludes that effective technology integration requires human-centered ecosystems that amplify, not replace, teacher agency, advancing a value-rational approach recognizing teachers’ professional flourishing as an intrinsic good rather than an instrumental means.

Purpose This study systematically examines the intersection of emotional intelligence (EI), leadership and learning-oriented development to understand how the field has evolved and its implications for human resource development (HRD) theory and practice. Design/methodology/approach A bibliometric analysis of 72 Scopus-indexed, ABDC-ranked journal articles published between 2015 and 2025 was conducted using Bibliometrix and VOSviewer. The analysis examined publication trends, collaboration networks, keyword co-occurrence patterns and thematic evolution within the field. Findings Seven thematic clusters emerged, with EI functioning as a central construct linking leadership, workplace learning and organizational outcomes. The findings indicate a shift from viewing EI as a fixed trait to conceptualizing it as a developable capability shaped through learning, reflection and relational experiences. The field has evolved from early conceptual exploration (2015–2018) to more empirical and context-driven research, particularly in the postpandemic period (2022–2025). While transformational leadership and EI remain dominant themes, adaptive, digital and crisis leadership have emerged as important areas of inquiry. The analysis also reveals a geographically diverse research landscape, although international collaboration remains uneven across regions. Originality/value This study provides a comprehensive bibliometric overview of the intersection between EI, leadership and learning and advances a learning-oriented perspective by positioning EI as a key capability within leadership development frameworks. By integrating leadership, workplace learning and organizational context, the study contributes to HRD and leadership scholarship and offers a structured foundation for future research and practice.

Purpose This study aims to examine the trends, intellectual structure, frequently explored topics, and future research directions in employee engagement within small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs), thereby providing insights for theoretical development and HRM practice. Design/methodology/approach This review applied bibliometric methods to examine 730 documents indexed in the Scopus database and published between 1989 and 2024. The study utilized descriptive analyses and science mapping techniques, including co-citation and keyword co-occurrence analyses. Findings The findings reveal growing academic interest, highlighting a shift from transactional to transformational human resource management. Further research in South America and Africa is needed to improve the generalizability of the existing knowledge base. Three main clusters were identified along with influential authors and key theories in each area: “Integrated Psychological and Occupational Health”, “Dynamic Organizational Studies”, and “Work Engagement and Burnout”. Temporal co-word analysis shows the enduring relevance of job satisfaction and organizational commitment, with an emerging focus on the impacts of COVID-19 and sustainability, including corporate social responsibility (CSR), reflecting a trend toward integrating sustainable practices into business strategies. Originality/value To the authors' knowledge, this is the first bibliometric review focused specifically on employee engagement in the SME context, an important HRM issue for the effective management of human resources.

Using adaptive intelligence as a theoretical lens, the study investigates how L2 motivational selves are associated with AI-IDLE engagement through psychological capital (PsyCap) and L2 grit and whether these indirect associations vary with AI literacy among 1025 Chinese university EFL learners. The proposed model was tested using structural equation modeling (SEM). For the ideal L2 self, associations with engagement emerged both directly and indirectly through PsyCap and L2 grit, whereas the ought-to L2 self showed an indirect association through PsyCap and no direct association with engagement. Higher AI literacy corresponded to stronger associations of both PsyCap and L2 grit with engagement. The two motivational self-guides were therefore associated with engagement through different psychological pathways, with AI literacy related to variation in the strength of these pathways. From an adaptive intelligence perspective, this conditional pattern indicates that the relevance of PsyCap and L2 grit to AI-IDLE engagement varies with learners’ AI literacy. These findings extend the application of adaptive intelligence to informal human–AI learning.

Modern English as a Foreign Language (EFL) pronunciation instruction has shifted its primary goal from native-like accent imitation to functional intelligibility and comprehensibility. Despite this paradigm shift, traditional classroom settings often struggle to provide personalized, real-time diagnostic feedback due to large class sizes and time constraints. This study investigates the pedagogical integration of Artificial Intelligence (AI)-driven speech analysis and automated acoustic feedback in EFL pronunciation teaching. Synthesizing contemporary literature on Computer-Assisted Pronunciation Training (CAPT) and feedback literacy, this paper examines how AI feedback impacts learner autonomy, segmental clarity, and suprasegmental awareness. The review reveals that AI tools provide consistent, low-anxiety practice environments that facilitate cognitive noticing and self-correction. However, over-reliance on automated metrics without explicit pedagogical framing can result in mechanical practice detached from communicative contexts. To reconcile these dynamics, this article introduces a conceptual Scaffolded Pedagogical Feedback Model (SPFM) that integrates AI-generated acoustic diagnostic data, structured peer dialogue, and teacher-mediated instructional intervention. The framework highlights the necessity of developing student feedback literacy to transform automated output into actionable learning strategies. Keywords: EFL pronunciation instruction, Computer-Assisted Pronunciation Training (CAPT), artificial intelligence, intelligibility, learner autonomy, feedback literacy.

This community service activity aimed to improve the understanding of senior high school and vocational high school students regarding classroom chair design based on anthropometric principles. The activity was conducted face-to-face at partner schools in Jakarta through ergonomics lectures, demonstrations of seated anthropometric measurements, percentile calculation exercises, and discussions on applying measurement results to chair dimensions. The anthropometric dimensions introduced included popliteal height, buttock-popliteal length, hip breadth, sitting shoulder height, and sitting elbow height. Evaluation was conducted through pre-tests and post-tests, question-and-answer sessions, observation of practical activities, analysis, and reflection. The results showed an improvement in participants’ understanding of anthropometric dimensions relevant to chair design. The proportion of participants who provided fully correct answers increased from 42.0% in the pre-test to 83.3% in the post-test. Participants were also able to identify the relationship between body dimensions and chair components, explain the risks associated with dimensional mismatch, and formulate initial principles for determining seat height, seat depth, seat width, and backrest dimensions. The activity demonstrated that contextual, practice-based learning can enhance students’ ergonomic literacy and encourage data-based thinking in evaluating learning facilities.

The rapid integration of generative AI tools has transformed writing instruction, raising questions about authorship, agency, and academic integrity in teacher education. Unlike search engines, generative AI produces synthesized text that supports brainstorming, drafting, revising, and feedback. While these tools can reduce cognitive load and enhance higher-order thinking, they may also weaken productive struggle, writer identity, and promote overreliance without intentional instructional design. These issues are especially relevant for preservice teachers who must learn to use AI both ethically and instructionally. Grounded in self-regulation, self-efficacy, metacognitive theory, and the cognitive process model of writing, this study frames AI as metacognitive scaffolding for writing development. The framework highlights a gap between preservice teachers' frequent use of AI and their limited readiness to teach with it. The article argues that intentional, theory-driven integration can support planning, monitoring, and reflection while preserving student voice and autonomy. I

Digital tools for eating-disorder support often rely on retrospective self-report or text-based prompts, offering limited support for the embodied, temporally unfolding nature of eating episodes. We introduce Embodied Therapeutic Interaction (ETI), a design framework for translating CBT-informed principles into phase-aligned, behavior-aware interactions, and instantiate it in EnjoyEAT, a prototype combining surface electromyography sensing with pre-meal preparation, in-meal awareness cues, and post-meal reflection. Formative inquiry with experts and people with lived experience yielded requirements concerning temporal vulnerability, bodily awareness, emotional safety, and autonomy-preserving feedback. A four-week, uncontrolled in-the-wild study with 12 participants reporting subclinical tendencies showed decreased EDE-Q scores and positive user-experience ratings. Interviews indicated feedback helped some participants notice and reflect on eating patterns, while revealing tensions around sensing accuracy, setup burden, and sustained engagement. Though not a clinical intervention, EnjoyEAT offers HCI design evidence about phase alignment, soft embodiment, reflective mediation, and emotionally careful feedback for situated recovery support.

This working paper examines whether the classical methodology of ʿilal al-Ḥadīth—the detection of hidden defects in apparently sound reports—can provide a useful conceptual framework for evaluating artificial-intelligence outputs in specialist knowledge environments. It develops the concept of the “epistemic hidden defect”: a weakness in provenance, attribution, inference, context, evidential hierarchy, or scholarly status that may remain concealed beneath a fluent and apparently authoritative AI-generated response. Drawing on classical Hadith-critical methodology and contemporary AI research, the paper distinguishes computational capability from scholarly authority. It develops the concepts of the Authority Ceiling, Digital Isnād, competence-specific human oversight, and the No-Autonomous-Grading Principle as safeguards for AI-assisted scholarship. The paper argues for an AI-assisted rather than AI-autonomous model of specialist research, in which computational systems widen the evidential field while consequential scholarly judgement remains traceable, reviewable, and accountable.
