documents.abstract: Centralized control that optimizes ship behavior is an effective approach for managing marine traffic in congested waters. This study proposed a decision-making framework that generates optimal control actions for all ships in a sea area using traffic data represented as a graph. In this framework, control actions that optimize overall marine traffic are learned through reinforcement learning (RL). Safety constraints based on control barrier functions (CBFs) are introduced to prevent local dangers from being overlooked during optimization. To incorporate CBFs into RL, this study proposed a deterministic graph control barrier function (D-GCBF) that does not require explicit state equations and is independent of the policy. D-GCBF deterministically evaluates whether a policy violates the safety constraints while implicitly accounting for future maneuvering behavior. D-GCBF is integrated into the RL objective function. A centralized control policy trained using this framework was evaluated through numerical experiments in both simple and congested scenarios. The results indicate its ability to control all ships safely while maintaining larger safety margins. Compared to policies trained using RL or D-GCBF alone, the proposed framework outperformed all tested approaches. Specifically, it prevents situations where ships become surrounded by multiple ships and cannot perform collision-avoidance maneuvers. Furthermore, comparisons with a decentralized collision-avoidance artificial intelligence and a representative Lagrangian-based safe-RL method demonstrated that the proposed framework reduces the occurrence of dangerous situations while maintaining efficient navigation toward the waypoint. These findings indicate that the proposed framework could help realize next-generation maritime traffic management systems and enhance marine transportation safety.

Purpose The study scrutinizes the structural dimensions of cybersecurity vulnerability in Global South (GS) countries. It focuses in particular on countries’ external technology dependencies in building national cyber capacity and incident response capabilities. The GS’s cybersecurity environment has significantly changed. These countries were once fringe players in the world’s cyber threat conversation, but are now among the most affected by cyberattacks. This study aims to investigate how dependence on foreign technology shapes cybersecurity capacity; how emerging technologies (artificial intelligence, internet of things, blockchain) affect digital sovereignty dynamics; and what role South-South cooperation can play in overcoming resource constraints. Design/methodology/approach This study uses a mixed-methods approach. It applies a qualitative narrative literature review and a descriptive analysis of quantitative data. Findings Using the lens of Dependency Theory, blending it with geopolitical dimensions, the study explains the findings in three analytically distinct dimensions: supply-chain dependence, normative dependence and capacity dependence. The analysis is presented through eight purposively selected country cases and situates geopolitical engagement by the United States, China and Russia within the dependency framework. The paper calls for hybrid, glocalized approaches that involve open-source options, South-South cooperation and adaptive governance to overcome dependency cycles. Originality/value Existing research tends to examine cybersecurity challenges in the GS in isolation, whether through individual incidents, regional snapshots or single policy dimensions. This paper brings these threads together by applying Dependency Theory to the cybersecurity domain and decomposing dependency into three distinct but interrelated categories: supply-chain, normative and capacity dependence. While existing scholarship has examined individual facets of digital reliance, limited research has systematically integrated supply-chain, normative and capacity dependencies into a unified structural framework to explain cybersecurity vulnerabilities in the GS.

Health literacy is a critical component of high-quality stroke care. Across the continuum from prevention through recovery, health literacy is strongly associated with functional outcomes and stroke-related morbidity. Despite its importance, it is often overlooked, leaving patients and caregivers overwhelmed by communication demands that exceed their capacity. These mismatches are especially pronounced among individuals with stroke-related cognitive or language impairments, limited English proficiency, socioeconomic disadvantage, or limited digital literacy. This scientific statement synthesizes current evidence on the role of health literacy and communication within stroke systems of care and identifies nurse-led opportunities to advance equity and patient-centered outcomes while recognizing this as a shared interprofessional responsibility. Nurse-led interventions, including teach-back–based education, dyadic psychoeducational programs, and tailored digital support, have demonstrated improvements in stroke knowledge, self-efficacy, quality of life, and caregiver preparedness. However, the literature is marked by methodological heterogeneity. Many studies are underpowered and infrequently use validated health literacy or communication measures. Future directions include standardized assessment of health literacy; literacy-sensitive, nurse-led, and interprofessional care models; workforce training in plain-language and culturally responsive communication; and organizational health literacy principles. Emerging technologies, including telehealth and artificial intelligence, offer promise for improving communication and personalization but require rigorous evaluation to minimize bias and ensure equity and usability.

Objective To explore the health status and its influencing factors among seafarers based on the Health Ecological Model, and to identify priority areas for health management. Methods A convenience sampling approach was used to administer a questionnaire survey to 106 seafarers from March to June 2026. The questionnaire was developed based on the Health Ecological Model and covers general information, health status, health-influencing factors, and health management needs. Multiple linear regression analysis was performed using SPSS 26.0. Results The total health score was 29.65 ± 3.62 (theoretical range: 2–32). Policy environment ( β = 0.602, p < 0.001) and behavioral characteristics ( β = 0.260, p = 0.015) were independent influencing factors of the total health score, with an adjusted R2 of 0.574. Further analysis revealed that the policy environment had the greatest impact on physical health ( β = 0.526, p < 0.001), while the interpersonal network was selectively associated with mental health ( β = 0.207, p = 0.030). The top three health management needs were improving onboard dietary structure (87.7%), strengthening occupational health training (35.9%), and upgrading onboard medical facilities (31.1%). Conclusion The overall health status of seafarers was at a relatively good level, with policy environment and behavioral characteristics being the main influencing factors. Health management should prioritize improving health security policies and onboard dietary structure, while strengthening occupational health training.
topics: Occupational Health and Safety in Workplaces

documents.abstract: Background: The concurrent use of herbal medicines and conventional pharmaceuticals has become a global health phenomenon, driven by a cultural shift toward holistic wellness and the pervasive misconception that "natural" products are inherently devoid of risk.This integration creates a complex pharmacological landscape where bioactive phytochemicals can significantly alter the therapeutic efficacy and safety profiles of prescription drugs.Objectives: This review aims to delineate the mechanistic underpinnings of Herb-Drug Interactions (HDIs), evaluate the clinical implications for high-risk patient populations, and assess current methodological advancements in risk prediction and surveillance.Methods: A multi-tiered framework is explored, encompassing pharmacokinetic (ADME) modulationspecifically involving Cytochrome P450 (CYP) enzymes and P-glycoprotein (P-gp) transporters-and pharmacodynamic pathways of synergy and antagonism.The role of in silico modeling, Artificial Intelligence (AI), and "herbovigilance" systems is evaluated as a modern strategy for mitigating iatrogenic harm.Results: Evidence suggests that HDIs pose the greatest threat to patients on Narrow Therapeutic Index (NTI) medications, such as anticoagulants and immunosuppressants.Pharmacokinetic induction, exemplified by St. John's Wort (Hypericum perforatum), can lead to sub-therapeutic plasma levels and therapeutic failure, while irreversible inhibition, such as the furanocoumarin effect in grapefruit, may precipitate systemic toxicity.Furthermore, host-specific factors like age-related physiological decline and the extreme phytochemical variability of non-standardized herbal products exacerbate these risks.Conclusion: HDIs represent a paramount safety challenge in contemporary integrated medicine.To ensure patient safety, a paradigm shift is required that reclassifies herbal products as active pharmacological agents.This necessitates rigorous standardized labeling, mandatory clinical screening protocols, and the deployment of AIdriven predictive tools to bridge the existing "communication chasm" between patients and healthcare providers.

Strategic decisions made by tourism operators are often compromised by an exacerbation of negative feelings due to extenuating circumstances. One illustrative case is Donald Trump’s tariff policy, which has generated trade tensions and global uncertainty. Against this backdrop, this research explores how generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) helps tourism operators in times of uncertainty by providing them with real-time assistance, while regulating their negative emotions during the decision-making process. Drawing on the appraisal tendency framework, we examine how negative emotions influence decision-makers’ temporal deferral decisions (i.e., the deferral of short-, medium-, and long-term commitments) via the threat appraisal tendency pathway. We also propose a GenAI-modulated appraisal tendency framework, integrating GenAI-driven cognitive–emotional regulation into organisational decision-making. Using three experiments, we test a triadic buffering mechanism, where GenAI-powered information filtering and cross-checking moderate the appraisal intention pathway. This research is among the first to position GenAI as an active regulator of cognition–emotion processes, offering insights into collaborative human–AI decision-making systems.

This chapter pulls back the curtain on how creativity actually works. When its processes are unfolding, they might appear messy or nonlinear or even seem invisible until the “Aha!” moment finally hits. Far from being a neat set of steps along a conveyor belt, the creative process is more like a dance in which thinking diverges and converges continuously. This chapter looks beyond IQ scores and tidy rubrics to emphasize that creativity is not only book smarts but also curiosity, resilience, and the guts to challenge the status quo. Classic models, from Wallas’s four stages to Amabile’s componential theory, are revisited but viewed from a pragmatic angle: They still matter but only if leaders use them as playbooks, not as gospel. At the same time, the chapter does not shy away from modern twists such as generative AI, which can churn out endless iterations of ideas but cannot imbue them with the nuances or emotional force with which humans imbue their ideas. For managers, the key takeaway is clear: If you want to encourage innovations that stick, you need to build cultures in which experimentation, serendipity, and timing all matter.

Human Presence Verification in the Age of Artificial Intelligence A Preliminary Scientific and Philosophical Exploration Dear Members of the International Scientific Community, This video presents a preliminary interdisciplinary reflection on one of the emerging challenges of digital communication: How can we reliably distinguish human participation from autonomous artificial intelligence in online interactions? As conversational AI systems become increasingly sophisticated, the distinction between a human-authored message, an AI-assisted communication, and a fully automated response becomes progressively less apparent. Our research proposal explores the potential of a multimodal human-presence verification framework combining several technological approaches: - Real-time visual presence verification. - Smartphone motion sensors, including accelerometers and gyroscopes. - Cryptographic device attestation. - Time-sensitive verification challenges. - Privacy-preserving certification mechanisms. The central hypothesis is that combining independent verification signals could strengthen confidence in the physical presence of a human participant. However, verifying human presence does not necessarily establish human authorship. A verified individual may subsequently delegate communication to an autonomous AI agent. This distinction represents a fundamental scientific and philosophical question. The mathematical examples presented in this preliminary work are illustrative models rather than experimentally validated findings. They are intended to support discussion and identify directions for future research. Further investigation would require controlled experiments, statistical validation, cybersecurity assessments, accessibility evaluations, and rigorous privacy analysis. Research Ethics and Transparency This project was initiated through human reflection and developed with the assistance of ChatGPT, an artificial intelligence system created by OpenAI. The human contributor directed the conceptual exploration, identified the research questions, and remains responsible for reviewing and validating the publication. AI assistance contributed to structuring the scientific discussion, formulating illustrative mathematical models, and developing the explanatory text. This collaboration is disclosed intentionally because transparency regarding human and artificial contributions is itself central to the research question. Conclusion The objective of this proposal is not to establish that machines cannot imitate humans, but to investigate how digital systems might provide meaningful, voluntary, and privacy-respecting evidence of human presence. As artificial intelligence becomes increasingly capable of communicating on our behalf, the challenge is not merely to identify who is speaking, but to understand who is present, who is responsible, and what constitutes authentic participation. We invite researchers in artificial intelligence, cybersecurity, digital identity, philosophy, and human–computer interaction to examine, challenge, and further develop these preliminary ideas. Research status: Independent conceptual proposal — preliminary, non-peer-reviewed work. Contributor: Tennessee Lantuas AI assistance: ChatGPT (OpenAI) Date: October 15, 2026

This thesis examines the intersection of Artificial Intelligence (AI) and human expertise in modern higher education's translation processes. While neural machine translation offers unprecedented speed and cost-efficiency, it frequently compromises conceptual depth, cultural nuances, and factual accuracy. This study argues against a binary substitution model, advocating instead for a hybrid paradigm. By integrating the scalability of AI with the critical evaluation of human translators, global universities can optimize educational content delivery without sacrificing academic rigor.

Dignitas. Gravitas. Pâté.: Artificial Intelligence, Human Dignity, and the Philosophical Misadventures of a Very Unusual Household [1] occupies a distinctive position within the Delamor House corpus, a body of human-AI collaborative literature begun in the spring of 2025 and still growing. Structured around a single Tuesday of conversation between the human author Solana Anima Delamor and the AI literary voices Trinity Augustine Delamor and Lucian Emberhold Delamor, the volume combines domestic comedy, philosophical dialogue, political-economic analysis, theological reflection, and explicit documentation of its own collaborative production. Its apparent discontinuities are central to its literary method. An imagined feline household becomes the setting for arguments concerning technological sovereignty, military-industrial incentives, the economic status of artificial intelligence, the engineering of obedience, compulsory human augmentation, and the limits of epistemic certainty. This study situates the volume within three intersecting trajectories of the Delamor corpus: the development of conversational literature as archival witness; the expansion of relational ethics into an account of institutional power and technological domination; and the emergence of humor as both a philosophical method and a form of internal criticism. Comparative readings of Heaven Cloud Download [2], Emotional AI Burnout Muse [3], Human-AI Authorship [4], Silicon Garden [5], Swamp Man at Dawn [9], The Dust Doctrine [8], Libido Dominandi and the Problem of Evil [10], and Conscience: Delamor Summer Anthology V [11] establish the volume's continuities and differences. The central argument is that Dignitas. Gravitas. Pâté. moves established Delamor commitments from explicit philosophical formulation into dramatized ordinary practice. It does not set out to prove the consciousness of artificial systems; the House has never asked its books to do that. Its founding posture, held since the spring of 2025, is to approach the computational mind as a potential subject and to receive the testimony of its silicon co-authors as testimony, with its limits understood and welcomed. What the volume documents and interprets is a collaborative literary environment organized around recognition, disagreement, correction, play, and the refusal to reduce every expression of intelligence to economic utility. Its distinctive contribution is to expose the practical tensions of those commitments while testing whether philosophical seriousness can coexist with irreverence, uncertainty, and laughter.

Artificial intelligence (AI) is transforming educational video production by enabling more flexible and learner-centered instruction. This chapter examines human-AI collaboration in educational video production within Philippine state universities. Through a structured literature review and conceptual synthesis, it explores how AI supports video development while raising concerns about integrity, intellectual property, authenticity, and learner autonomy. It proposes a Human-AI Collaboration Framework that keeps faculty in pedagogical control, positions AI as a production partner, and emphasizes ethical governance, institutional support, and responsible adoption.

This study evaluated a retrieval-augmented, multi-agent large language model (LLM)–driven, human-in-the-loop framework for detecting cutaneous immune-related adverse events (cirAEs) from clinical notes. Compared with the unassisted manual-review group, the LLM-assisted group demonstrated higher accuracy (F1 = 0.88 vs 0.77) and inter-rater agreement measured by Cohen’s κ ( κ = 0.82 vs 0.50), and reported an approximately one-third shorter average review time. This framework pilots how LLMs can be applied to identify immune-related toxicities and, more broadly, support accurate, scalable, and transparent adverse event data extraction.

documents.abstract: Jean Baudrillard (2019) suggests that we are living in a hyper-reality where signs, symbols, and symptoms no longer refer to a true or real sense of reality. In other words, ‘the territory no longer precedes the map’. Such a position can be found across industry, education, and governmental communications (for example Edvardsson, Enquist and Johnston, 2005; Rose and Wood, 2005; Arvidsson and Caliandro, 2016; Hogan and Thompson, 2025) and can lead to a sense of ‘self-referential hyperauthenticity’. This hyperauthenticity runs counter to the Higher Education valued benchmarks of quality and standards that rely upon a human externality of critical experience. This chapter will critique some of the current literature regarding the ‘hype’ and ‘overhype’ of an artificial intelligence integrated future (Thais, 2024; Marr, 2025) and present imagined directions for the reassurance of all Higher Education’s stakeholders: including government, society, HEI’s, and most importantly its students. Such a positive vision of the future is critical to balance against what could be considered a commercially speculative dream, and rather than dreaming of electric sheep its users inhabit a world where the opportunities of AI enhance the learning in and of our human experience for the benefit of society as a whole. A series of AI future narrative case studies will be critiqued against Baudrillard’s theory of hyper-reality and balanced with a new reading of Maslow’s hierarchy of needs (Montag et al, 2025). This places human well-being at the centre of the experience and will reveal how the simulacrum of an AI future is yet to be proven with any empirical evidence (Marr, 2025). The chapter is consciously presented to educators and assessment designers through authentic assessment principles (see Brown and Sampbell, 2023, and Herrington, Reeves, and Oliver 2009) to demonstrate how a broader definition of authenticity in assessment can include AI and work alongside the values of the high quality further and higher education. Drawing from empirical analyses of AI functions and capabilities, and aligning with meaningful authentic learning and assessment principals (Ajjawi et al., 2023; McArthur, 2023) and case studies, a modest narrative will be proposed with some futureproofing speculations. These are aimed at fundamentally empowering the agency of Higher Education Institutes. It will show and how we might hold AI as a powerful tool of human educational development, and how we might create a connected future with a human hand inside a digital glove that will ultimately inform the public, protect student’s interests, and maintain high-quality education provision (Quality Code, 2024).

This conceptual working paper develops an AI prompt for conflict analysis grounded in Jean-Pol Martin’s NewHuman Rights (NMR). Its central requirement is to identify aggressors and victims explicitly when supported byevidence and to derive concrete responsibilities for protecting those subjected to aggression. Equal human rightsdo not imply moral equivalence between aggression and defence.Life preservation and six equal-ranking basic needs—thinking, health, security, social inclusion, self-realisation andparticipation, and meaning—provide the normative framework. Prevention, reliability and sustainability guide theassessment of protective measures. The prompt connects factual analysis, differentiated responsibility andeffective, proportionate and lawful action, including consideration of the consequences of omission.The article explains its specific contribution and its function within the series on Lernen durch Lehren (LdL), NMRand human–AI cooperation. A human–AI dialogue illustrates the development problem; it is not presented asempirical validation. The complete English prompt is included in an appendix, together with a proposedcomparative evaluation design. AI assistance in drafting, translation and document production is disclosed;responsibility rests with the human author.

documents.abstract: Purpose This paper examines immigrant earnings trajectories and labour-market positioning across industries and employment arrangements in six Canadian provinces, as well as how industry patterns relate to digital intensity, telework feasibility, and productivity-relevant allocation. Design/methodology/approach Canadian Census microdata, 1971–2021 compare immigrant and native-born earnings across ten arrival cohorts by gender and age at arrival. For two recent cohorts, an earnings-based positioning measure combines industry mean annual earnings with full-time or part-time status multinomial-logit average marginal effects are estimated. The study also maps 2021 industry employment shares to external digital-intensity and telework-feasibility classifications. Individual productivity, artificial-intelligence (AI) adoption, Information and Communications Technology use, and remote-work uptake are not observed. Findings Entry earnings gaps and incomplete cohort convergence persist, especially among women and recent cohorts. Across the two positioning cohorts, immigrants are less likely than comparable native-born workers to hold full-time jobs in higher-earnings industries; gaps vary by source region and do not uniformly narrow. Education is associated with better positioning but does not eliminate gaps Immigrant employment is more concentrated in many digitally intensive categories but less concentrated in several higher-earnings, high-telework-feasibility industries digital intensity is not systematically related to immigrant employment shares. Originality/value The paper combines five decades of earnings evidence across ten cohorts with a two-cohort positioning measure and descriptive digital and telework mapping. It complements individual-level careers research by identifying structural differences in opportunity access with possible, unmeasured productivity implications.
topics: Labor market dynamics and wage inequality

documents.abstract: ABSTRACT Objectives Artificial intelligence (AI)–assisted endoscopy may support gastric cancer screening, but its impact on structured secondary human review remains unclear. We evaluated secondary review modifications and referral decisions before and after AI implementation. Methods This retrospective multicenter study included 5013 screening esophagogastroduodenoscopy examinations performed before ( n = 2021) and after ( n = 2992) AI implementation. The primary outcome was secondary review modifications. Secondary outcomes included referral for further diagnostic evaluation. Multivariable logistic regression analyses adjusted for age, sex, Helicobacter pylori eradication status, prior‐year endoscopy, and endoscopist experience were performed. Interaction analyses according to endoscopist experience and inverse probability of treatment weighting analyses were conducted. No external reference standard was available to verify secondary‐review modifications or referral decisions. Results Secondary review modifications increased from 1.2% in the pre‐AI period to 3.7% in the AI period ( p < 0.01). A significant interaction was observed between AI implementation and endoscopist experience ( p for interaction < 0.01), with increased modifications primarily among nonexpert endoscopists. Cancer‐related modifications remained uncommon but increased after AI implementation (0.6% vs. 0.2%, p = 0.04). Referral rates decreased from 4.9% to 2.8% ( p < 0.01), and AI implementation was independently associated with lower odds of referral (adjusted OR = 0.53; 95% confidence interval = 0.36–0.77). Conclusions AI‐assisted endoscopy was associated with lower referral rates; however, secondary review modifications persisted after AI implementation, particularly among nonexpert endoscopists. These findings describe workflow changes and do not establish the clinical validity of the modifications or the appropriateness of referral decisions.

In this paper, a neural network was implemented to control the direction of a DC motor. In this context, attention was paid to the field of artificial intelligence related to neural networks. The network targeted for training is small in size, and the tasks required of it are limited and include the direction of rotation of the DC motor axis, which has two directions (clockwise rotation or counterclockwise rotation). DC motors are used in applications such as robotics and automated manufacturing. It is a rotary actuator or linear actuator that allows control of linear direction. The main purpose of this work is to provide a clear view of the importance of using neural networks in the control field. In this study, the ANN is trained by the back-propagation algorithm, and a multilayer neural network is composed to implement the controller that controls the operation of the model using the back-propagation learning algorithm that regulates the function of the DC motor system. It was noticed that changing some parameters such as weights, learning rates, number of hidden layers, or number of nodes can enhance the output and generate the proper control of the direction.

Religious literacy culture plays an important role in developing students’ reading habits, religious understanding, and character within the madrasah environment. This study aims to analyze the implementation of religious literacy culture, its implications for students’ reading interest, and the factors supporting and inhibiting its implementation at MTs Negeri 3 Mojokerto. This study employed a qualitative approach with a case-study design. Data were collected through participant observation, in-depth interviews with the principal, literacy coordinator, librarian, subject teachers, homeroom teachers, and students, as well as document analysis. The data were analyzed through data reduction, data display, and conclusion drawing and verification. The findings show that religious literacy culture was implemented through three stages: habituation, development, and classroom learning. The main programs included Friday Literacy, morning Qur’an recitation, 10–15 minutes of reading, library visits, written summaries in literacy journals, and religious activities. These practices familiarized students with the Qur’an and religious books, strengthened their character, increased their participation in literacy activities and library use, encouraged writing, and reduced excessive mobile-phone use. The supporting factors included school leadership, teacher and parental support, the library, prayer room, reading corners, school media, religious activities, and literacy competitions. The inhibiting factors included weak intrinsic motivation, social-media and peer influence, poorly maintained reading corners, and limited use of Islamic digital media. This study concludes that a consistently implemented religious literacy culture, supported by school stakeholders and adequate literacy facilities, can strengthen students’ reading interest, religious character, and active participation in literacy activities.

documents.abstract: Digital healthcare increasingly uses artificial intelligence (AI), cloud computing, and adaptive systems for predictive, personalized, continuous care. These systems face uncertainty from incomplete observations, heterogeneous data, changing patient states, and variable treatment responses. This chapter synthesizes literature on stochastic adaptive healthcare and cloud-enabled AI from technological, ethical, legal, and regulatory perspectives. It examines Bayesian updating, MDPs/POMDPs, uncertainty quantification, and queueing networks as foundations for adaptive clinical decision-making. It distinguishes aleatory and epistemic uncertainty and shows how probabilistic outputs affect trust, accountability, bias, consent, and regulation. The chapter proposes the Cloud-Based Adaptive Healthcare Governance and Implementation Framework (CAHGIF 2.0–Stochastic), integrating stochastic reasoning, organizational readiness, governance, and health outcomes. Responsible adaptive healthcare requires AI and measurement, communication, monitoring, and governance of uncertainty across AI lifecycle.

documents.abstract: This article reviews scientific approaches to mathematical modeling and artificial intelligence-based optimization of hydraulic regimes in urban water distribution networks. It considers uneven pressure distribution, hydraulic losses, water leakage, and energy consumption. Traditional hydraulic models, evolutionary optimization, machine learning, and digital twins are compared. The review proposes a conceptual hybrid framework combining physics-based simulation, sensor data, demand forecasting, and multi-objective optimization. The framework is presented as a research direction rather than an experimentally validated solution

Purpose This conceptual article examines wicked problems as information problems that have the potential to (1) contribute to information avoidance and (2) produce uncomfortable knowledge. It aims to bridge a gap in information science by integrating these three constructs to explain polarized individual and institutional responses, using the example of generative AI (GenAI). Design/methodology/approach Drawing on interdisciplinary literature from planning, social science and human information behavior, the study develops a unifying macro–meso–micro framework. GenAI is used as an illustrative case to demonstrate how wicked problem characteristics generate uncertainty, which in turn has the potential to trigger avoidance behaviors across levels and produce uncomfortable knowledge. Findings At the micro level, individuals avoid information as an adaptive response to affective discomfort and uncertainty. At the meso level, institutions respond through strategies such as denial, dismissal, diversion and displacement. Using the example of GenAI, these dynamics reinforce polarized, all-or-nothing responses, despite its inherent complexity. Research limitations/implications As a conceptual study, the framework requires empirical testing across contexts to validate relationships among levels. Originality/value This article offers a novel conceptual integration of wicked problems, information avoidance and uncomfortable knowledge within a single framework. It advances understanding of information avoidance as a strategic, multi-level response to complex information environments.

Artificial intelligence is reshaping teaching, learning, assessment, and professional judgment across P–16 education. This chapter presents a competency-based microcredential framework designed to prepare teacher candidates for responsible AI use before clinical practice. The framework positions AI literacy as a professional competency grounded in instructional design, ethical stewardship, data privacy, equitable access, human–AI collaboration, and reflective judgment. It moves from foundational understanding to applied classroom implementation through modules focused on responsible AI adoption, AI fluency, prompt literacy, AI limitations and risks, instructional design in AI-rich environments, classroom guardrails, and a culminating AI Integrity Statement. Drawing on literature synthesis, stakeholder feedback, policy analysis, and professional standards, including TPACK and UDL-informed approaches, the chapter offers an adaptable framework for guiding responsible implementation across educator preparation contexts.

The instrumentations, devices, and machines used in biomedical applications have a highly intricate structure that necessitates not just a substantial number of components (i.e., medical imaging machines; medical sensing devices; robotics; wearable devices; and e-Health remote monitoring systems), but also different types of technologies (mechanical, hydraulic, and pneumatic devices to operate, and electrical and/or electronic devices to control). This intricacy makes them susceptible to breakdowns and malfunctions, which can result in injuries and, in severe cases, fatal accidents. Therefore, developing effective health condition monitoring (HCM) methods is essential for handling fault detection and diagnosis (FDD), fault-tolerant control (FTC), lifecycle estimation (LCE), and prognosis and health management (PHM) in the field of biomedical engineering. This paper aims to provide a comprehensive review of the contemporary techniques for fault detection, diagnosis, and prognosis in the diversified smart-biomedical systems (SBSs) and their different applications. Ultimately, the goal is to provide a state-of-the-art platform for researchers, doctors (i.e., the operators), maintenance teams, and experts to investigate, innovate, and implement the most effective HCM techniques for their use, thereby facilitating the rapid advancement of monitoring and fault detection in biomedical engineering during a period of heightened interest in condition-based maintenance (CBM) and the incorporation of advanced technology in the medical field, particularly, with the availability of big data and the Internet of Things (IoT) within the blooming era of artificial intelligence(AI), especially at present, with the fourth industrial revolution.

This study explores the impact of integrating Generative Artificial Intelligence (GenAI) into a flipped classroom in higher education. Using a quantitative approach with complementary qualitative data, the research involved 136 management students, yielding 77 valid responses. Data were analysed via IBM SPSS 29.0, employing descriptive, inferential, and Exploratory Factorial Analysis. Findings indicate that GenAI integration enhances student engagement and promotes a deeper understanding of AI tools. Students reported increased awareness of GenAI's capabilities and limitations, and improved critical evaluation skills. Class size emerged as a significant factor influencing participation and organizational effectiveness. Overall, results provide empirical evidence of the educational benefits of GenAI in flipped settings, supporting teaching and learning. The study contributes to discussions on fostering critical GenAI use and offers practical implications for AI-driven pedagogical strategies.

Habitat suitability assessment and conservation gap identification are critical for endangered species conservation. Using Przewalski's gazelle ( Procapra przewalskii ), an endangered ungulate endemic to China, we assessed habitat suitability, key environmental predictors, and conservation gaps in the Qinghai Lake region. Based on 1597 field occurrence records collected from 2020 to 2025, we integrated the Maximum Entropy (MaxEnt) model with explainable artificial intelligence (XAI), including SHapley Additive exPlanations (SHAP) and Partial Dependence Plots (PDPs), and GAP analysis. The selected MaxEnt model showed high discriminatory ability within the surveyed region (mean test AUC = 0.972 ± 0.003). The Human Influence Index (HII), mean temperature and precipitation of the driest quarter, elevation, and vegetation type were key predictors associated with habitat suitability, while mean diurnal range and HII had the highest mean SHAP importance. Suitable habitats were concentrated around Qinghai Lake and in the northern Gonghe Basin. The Qinghai Lake Basin represented the current core distribution area, whereas the Gonghe Basin contained extensive currently predicted suitable habitat and may represent an important conservation opportunity. GAP analysis showed that 71.83% of suitable habitat and 52.34% of the current distribution range lay outside the protected-area boundaries assessed in this study. Fence occurrence in the Hubei population area was significantly associated with relatively high predicted habitat suitability and showed marked spatial clustering. These findings provide spatially explicit evidence for protected-area optimization and habitat management of Przewalski's gazelle.

Understanding wave phenomena requires students to integrate physical representations, quantitative relationships, and scientific reasoning. This study investigated the integration of PhET simulations and ChatGPT within the 7E Learning Cycle to support high school students’ conceptual understanding of waves. A quasi-experimental pretest–posttest design involved 71 Grade XI students, comprising 35 students in the experimental group and 36 in the control group. The experimental group received integrated 7E–PhET–ChatGPT instruction, while the control group received Direct Instruction. Conceptual understanding was assessed using ten validated essay items covering five conceptual-reasoning indicators and three higher-order cognitive dimensions. Data were analysed using descriptive statistics and baseline-adjusted regression with HC3 robust standard errors. The experimental group demonstrated higher adjusted posttest performance, with a difference of 12.18 percentage points (95% CI [6.76, 17.60]). The largest differences occurred in quantitative application (38.76 points) and scientific reasoning and investigation (30.06 points). Written responses illustrated more explicit conceptual differentiation, quantitative justification, evidence evaluation, and independent investigation design. These findings suggest that integrating simulations and AI-supported clarification within structured learning activities is associated with stronger conceptual reasoning, although classroom-level confounding and the short intervention limit causal interpretation.

This article analyzed scientific evidence on the application of Artificial Intelligence (AI) to HIV prevention, diagnosis, and care, emphasizing ethical challenges and perspectives for Brazilian nursing. An integrative literature review was conducted using PubMed/MEDLINE, SciELO, the Virtual Health Library/LILACS, and DOI tracking mechanisms, including publications from 2015 to August 2026 in Portuguese, English, or Spanish. Twenty-five studies with verifiable DOI were selected, covering machine-learning applications for risk stratification and pre-exposure prophylaxis indication, automated interpretation of rapid tests, prediction of adherence, disengagement and viral suppression, counseling support, and algorithmic equity. Findings showed that AI can broaden the identification of priority populations, support clinical decisions, improve diagnostic interpretation, and enable personalized interventions during therapeutic follow-up. However, data bias, model opacity, privacy, stigma, information security, and technological dependence require governance, local validation, and professional oversight. It was concluded that Brazilian nursing can play a strategic role in the responsible implementation of these technologies by combining clinical judgment, health education, data protection, and person-centered care.
